theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why is a welded frame inspected at stages during the work, and not only when it is finished?
options: So the inspector has more forms to fill in at the end
Faults are found while they are cheap to put right
So the welders need not read the drawing at all
Because clients never allow a final inspection

questions.stem: Where would you find the limits for weld faults that may be accepted on a job at the Centre?
options: In the welder's own notebook from last year
On the label of the electrode packet
In the maker's manual for the welding machine
In the code or procedure the job names

questions.stem: On a fabrication job, what does the inspection and test plan set out?
options: A list of each check, when it is done and who signs
A drawing showing the shape of every part to make
A price list for testing done by outside firms
A timetable of the welders' breaks during the job

questions.stem: A plan says no root run may start until the inspector has checked and signed the fit-up. What is this kind of stage called?
options: A witness point
A review point
A hold point
A rest point

questions.stem: Why is the heat number stamped on delivered steel plate recorded and checked against the mill certificate?
options: To show how hot the plate got in the sun
To check the weight of the plate before paying
So the plate can be traced to its test results
So the plate can be sold on later at a profit

questions.stem: A delivery of 10 mm plate is checked with a vernier caliper. One plate measures 8.6 mm. What should you do?
options: Quarantine it, label it and report it
Use it, as plate sizes always vary a little
Use it only on the less important parts
Grind the other plates down to match it

questions.stem: A packet of low-hydrogen electrodes arrives torn open and damp. What is the right action?
options: Use them at once before they get any wetter
Dry them in the sun on the bench for a day
Put them straight in the holder and weld as normal
Set them aside and follow the maker's rules

questions.stem: Which items are checked at the fit-up of a single-V butt joint, before any welding?
options: The cap height and the colour of the weld
Root gap, bevel angle, root face, alignment
The number of electrodes used and their cost
The paint thickness on the finished joint

questions.stem: Two pipes set up for a butt weld are out of line, so one wall stands higher than the other at the root. What is this called?
options: Undercut
Overlap
Underfill
Hi-lo

questions.stem: Why are tack welds inspected before the root run is laid over them?
options: Tacks are always ground off before welding
A cracked tack can pass its crack into the weld
Tacks are made with a different electrode
Checking tacks shows how fast the welder is

questions.stem: The WPS calls for a preheat of 100 °C. How can the inspector check it before welding starts?
options: Touch the plate quickly with a bare hand
Look for the plate turning a dull red
Use a temperature crayon or contact thermometer
Ask the welder how long the torch was on it

questions.stem: Why does the inspector compare the welding current and travel speed with the WPS while welding is going on?
options: They control heat input, fusion and strength
They show how tired the welder is getting
They decide how much the whole job will cost
They show whether the machine is a new one

questions.stem: Why must slag be fully removed between the runs of a multi-run weld?
options: Slag left behind is trapped as an inclusion
Slag makes the next run cool down too fast
Slag makes the weld look a darker colour
Slag uses up the shielding gas too quickly

questions.stem: Before a welder starts on a job that must meet a code, what does the inspector check?
options: That the welder owns his own helmet and gloves
That the welder has been at the Centre longest
That he is qualified for that process and position
That the welder has eaten lunch before starting

questions.stem: Which tools are most useful for the visual inspection of finished welds?
options: A hammer, a cold chisel and a pair of pliers
Good light, a magnifier, a mirror, weld gauges
A tape measure and a can of marking paint only
A multimeter and a set of feeler gauges

questions.stem: Why should welds be cleaned of slag and spatter before visual inspection?
options: Clean welds weigh less on the scale
The inspector likes welds to look shiny
So that paint can go on straight away
Slag and spatter can hide surface faults

questions.stem: A fillet weld has undercut 1.5 mm deep. The acceptance limit for the job is 0.5 mm. What is your decision?
options: Accept it, as undercut is only on the surface
Reject it and record it for repair
Accept it if the leg length is correct
Grind the cap flat, then accept it

questions.stem: Which surface finding is usually NOT accepted at any size in a structural weld?
options: Light spatter that brushes off easily
A slightly uneven ripple on the cap
A small change in the width of the cap
A crack

questions.stem: A row of MIG welds shows surface porosity. Which cause should be checked first?
options: Loss of shielding gas, for example a draught
The wire speed set a little too low for the job
The plate being too thick for that joint type
The welder holding the gun too steady and still

questions.stem: A drawing calls for an 8 mm fillet weld. How does the inspector check its leg length?
options: By eye, comparing it with a pencil
With a tape measure laid along the weld
With a fillet weld gauge on each leg
By weighing the electrode stubs used

questions.stem: A fillet weld measures 6 mm on the leg where 8 mm was called for. What is the risk if it is accepted?
options: The weld will be too heavy for the frame
The paint will not cover the weld properly
The joint may not be strong enough
The weld will take longer to cool down

questions.stem: Why is too much cap height (excess reinforcement) on a butt weld a fault, and not a bonus?
options: It causes stress at the toes and wastes filler
It makes the joint stronger than the plate
It makes the weld rust faster than the plate
It means the root was never welded at all

questions.stem: How would you inspect the root of a pipe butt weld that you cannot see directly?
options: Tap the outside of the pipe with a hammer
Ask the welder whether the root went through
Measure the cap width and judge the root
Use a mirror and torch, or a borescope

questions.stem: A welded gate frame is 1800 mm × 1200 mm. Its diagonals measure 2160 mm and 2172 mm. What does this tell you?
options: It is square, as both readings are over 2 m
It is out of square by a clear amount
It is twisted, but still perfectly square
It is too long and must be cut down

questions.stem: The drawing gives a frame length of 1500 mm ± 2 mm. You measure 1503 mm. What is the result?
options: Pass, as 3 mm is very small on 1.5 m
Pass, as long as the frame is square
Pass, if the next frame is 1497 mm long
Fail; record it as out of tolerance

questions.stem: Why must the tapes and weld gauges used for inspection be checked for accuracy?
options: So they can be sold for a good price later
So the readings taken with them can be trusted
So the inspector may use any tape that is near
Because a new tape is never accurate

questions.stem: A weld gauge used last week is found to be bent and reading 1 mm small. What should the inspector do?
options: Nothing, as last week's welds are now painted
Keep using it, adding 1 mm to every reading
Withdraw it and recheck the welds it measured
Throw it away and say nothing to anyone

questions.stem: Which test finds surface-breaking cracks in a stainless steel weld, where magnetic methods cannot be used?
options: Dye penetrant
Magnetic particle
Hardness testing
Spark testing

questions.stem: Who should carry out and interpret radiographic (X-ray) or ultrasonic tests on welds?
options: Technicians qualified in that test method
Any welder who has watched it being done
The trainee who welded that particular joint
The customer's driver when he collects it

questions.stem: Why are some butt welds given ultrasonic or radiographic tests as well as a visual inspection?
options: These tests are cheaper and faster than looking
These tests give the welder's name and number
They find faults inside the weld that eyes cannot
These tests clean the weld ready for painting

questions.stem: A job has 200 identical fillet welds. The ITP asks for 100% visual inspection and 10% dye penetrant. How many welds get dye penetrant?
In a 10% dye penetrant sample, two of the welds show cracks. What is the best next step?
options: Pass the job, as most of the welds were good
Repair the two and pass the rest unchecked
Paint all the welds and send the job out
Test more welds and look for the cause

questions.stem: What should be done with a fabricated part that fails inspection?
options: Send it to the customer with a discount
Mark it, keep it apart and record the fault
Hide it under other parts in the store
Cut it up for scrap straight away

questions.stem: What should a non-conformance report (NCR) about a weld record?
options: Only the welder's name and his rate of pay
The price of the steel and the delivery date
Only the colour of the paint to be used on it
The fault, its place, the requirement, the action

questions.stem: A rejected weld has been repaired. What must happen before the part is released?
options: It is inspected again to the same standard
Nothing, as the welder has now fixed it
It is painted so the repair cannot be seen
The customer is told it was never rejected

questions.stem: How does a weld map (a drawing with every weld numbered) help inspection?
options: It shows the shortest route around the shop
It lists the price of every weld on the job
Each weld's welder and results can be traced
It shows where to put the welding machines

questions.stem: A trainee writes four entries on a weld inspection sheet. Which entry gives the most useful information?
options: Weld looks OK to me
Some of the welds are bad
W12: 6 mm leg, needs 8 mm; reject
Will be fixed later on

questions.stem: You find a crack in a lifting lug on a frame that is due to be lifted today. When should you report it?
options: At once, and stop the lift until it is sorted
At the end of the week in the summary report
Only if the customer asks about it later on
After the lift, so the job is not held up

questions.stem: What should an inspector wear when watching a welder at work to check the settings and technique?
options: Ordinary dark sunglasses and a cap
Nothing extra if standing 1 m away
A dust mask and ear plugs, nothing else
Filter eye protection and suitable PPE

questions.stem: Why should you check that a weld has cooled before inspecting it by hand?
options: Hot welds always look bigger than they are
Hot steel can burn you without looking hot
Undercut only grows to full size as it cools
Paint must be dry before you can inspect

questions.stem: Dye penetrant sprays are to be used inside a small tank. What precaution is needed?
options: Use extra spray so the job is done faster
Spray it while a welder works close by
Leave the caps off the cans so they can breathe
Ventilation, no ignition, and PPE from the SDS

questions.stem: Why is good lighting important for the visual inspection of welds?
options: It keeps the inspector warm in the shop
Fine cracks and pores are missed in poor light
It helps the finished welds cool down faster
It makes the welds look a better colour

questions.stem: A welder in your team keeps leaving undercut on vertical welds. What is the best Level 3 action?
options: Accept the welds, because he works quickly
Report him to the Centre's manager at once
Show him the fault and its cause; check again
Do all his vertical welds for him from now on

questions.stem: Before a fabricated item is released to the customer, what does the final inspection confirm?
options: That every ITP check is done and signed
That the welders have been paid for the job
That the item is the same colour as the last one
That the delivery truck has enough fuel in it

questions.stem: A weld size on the drawing does not agree with the size in the job specification. Which action is right for the inspector?
options: Raise the query with the person in charge
Pick the smaller size to save time on the job
Pick whichever size the welder would prefer
Ignore both and go by the current on the WPS

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for the distance from the root of a fillet weld to its toe, measured along the face of the plate?
What name is given to the fault where weld metal has not melted into the parent metal or into the run below it?
What document from the steel maker gives the chemical and strength test results for a batch of steel?
What marker melts at a set temperature and is used to check that the preheat has been reached?
What two words describe tests, such as dye penetrant or ultrasonic, that check a weld without damaging it?
What is the name for the temperature of the weld area just before the next run is laid, which the WPS may limit?
The diagonals of a welded frame measure 2125 mm and 2131 mm. What is the difference between them, in millimetres?
What do we call the marked area where rejected or doubtful material is kept so that it cannot be used by mistake?
What name is given to the mark left on the plate surface, away from the weld, where an electrode was struck by mistake?
A sample of 40 welds is tested and 3 fail. What percentage fail?
In weld testing, what do the letters MPI stand for?
On an ITP, what is the name of a stage the client is invited to watch, but where work need not stop if they do not come?
What is the name for the shortest distance from the root of a fillet weld to its face?
What name is given to weld metal that spills over onto the plate at the toe without fusing to it?
What hand-held lens is used to look closely at a weld surface for very fine cracks?

essays.stem: Your team will fabricate a steel staircase for a guest house in Negril. Explain how you would plan the inspections from the delivery of materials to handover.
essays.modelAnswer: I write an inspection and test plan (ITP) for the job. First I read the drawings, the specification and the code or procedure the job names, so I know the acceptance limits. The plan lists each stage, what is checked, how, against what limit, who checks and who signs. Stage one is goods-in: steel sizes, grades, heat numbers and mill certificates, and the condition of electrodes and gas. Stage two is cutting and fit-up: sizes, bevels, root gaps and alignment, with a hold point so no welding starts until the fit-up is signed. Stage three is in-process: welder qualifications, settings against the WPS, preheat if needed and cleaning between runs. Stage four is final: visual weld inspection with gauges, any dye penetrant the specification asks for, and full dimensional checks such as rise, going and squareness. I mark witness points for the client, and the last stage checks that every record is complete before handover.
markingPoints: Reads drawings, specification and code to find acceptance limits
Writes an ITP listing stage, check, method, limit and who signs
Includes goods-in and fit-up checks with a hold point
Includes in-process and final visual, NDT and dimensional checks
Uses witness points and checks records complete before handover

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a delivery of steel plate, sections and welding consumables before they are given out, and what you would do with anything that fails.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the delivery note against the purchase order for the items and quantities. For the steel, I check the section sizes and plate thicknesses with a tape and vernier caliper, look for bends, deep pitting, laminations at cut edges and heavy rust, and check that the grade and heat numbers marked on the steel match the mill certificates. I keep the certificates with the job records. For consumables, I check the type and size of electrodes and wire against the WPS, the batch numbers and that the packets are sealed and dry; low-hydrogen electrodes go straight into the holding oven. I check gas cylinders for the right gas, labels and test dates. Anything that fails is labelled, moved to the quarantine area and recorded, and the supplier or the person in charge is told so that it can be replaced. Good material is booked into the store so it can be traced.
markingPoints: Checks delivery against the order
Measures and inspects steel; matches heat numbers to certificates
Checks consumables against the WPS and their condition and storage
Labels, quarantines and records anything that fails, and reports it
Books good items in and keeps certificates for traceability

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would make before and during the welding of a multi-run single-V butt joint, and why each check matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Before welding, I check the joint against the drawing and WPS. The bevel angle, root face and root gap must be right, because they control whether the root fuses through. I check alignment with a hi-lo gauge, because a step at the root gives lack of penetration. I check that the joint is clean of rust, paint and oil, which cause porosity, and that the tacks are sound and their ends feathered. I check that the welder is qualified for the process and position, and that the electrodes are the right type and dry. During welding, I check the preheat with a temperature crayon if the WPS asks for it, and the current, voltage and travel speed against the WPS, because they control heat input and fusion. I check that slag is removed from each run so it is not trapped, and that the interpass temperature stays inside the limit. I record the readings on the inspection sheet.
markingPoints: Checks bevel, root face and root gap with reasons
Checks alignment, cleanliness and tacks with reasons
Checks welder qualification and consumables
Checks preheat, settings against the WPS and interpass temperature
Checks cleaning between runs and records readings

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a visual inspection of the finished fillet welds on a fabricated frame. Include the tools, what you look for and how you decide to accept or reject.
essays.modelAnswer: I make sure the welds are cool and cleaned of slag and spatter, and that I have good light. My tools are a torch, a mirror, a magnifier, fillet weld gauges, a steel rule and the drawing with the acceptance limits. I check that every weld on the drawing is there, in the right place and of the right length. I measure the leg length and throat with the fillet gauge and compare them with the drawing. I look at the profile: it should be even, without too much convexity or concavity. I look for cracks, undercut, porosity, overlap, incomplete fill at the ends, arc strikes and heavy spatter. Each finding is compared with the limit in the code or procedure the job names. If it is inside the limit, it is accepted; if not, it is marked on the weld, recorded and rejected for repair. Any crack is rejected. I record the results for each weld number.
markingPoints: Prepares: cool, clean welds and good light
Lists suitable tools
Checks presence, position, length and size with gauges
Looks for the main surface faults
Compares with stated limits, marks and records rejects; any crack rejected

essays.stem: Explain the likely causes of porosity, undercut, lack of fusion and cracking in welds, and how an inspector would find each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Porosity is gas trapped in the weld. It is caused by loss of shielding gas, draughts, damp electrodes, or rust, oil and paint on the joint. Surface porosity is seen by eye; buried porosity needs radiography. Undercut is a groove melted into the plate at the toe and left unfilled. It comes from too much current, too fast travel or a poor electrode angle. It is seen by eye and its depth is measured with a gauge. Lack of fusion is weld metal not melted into the side wall or the run below. It comes from too little current, too fast travel, a wrong angle or slag left on the run before. It is often hidden, so ultrasonic testing or a bend test finds it, though it can show at the surface. Cracks come from fast cooling, high restraint, hydrogen from damp electrodes or poor material. Surface cracks are found by eye, dye penetrant or magnetic particle testing; inside cracks need ultrasonic or radiography.
markingPoints: Porosity: correct causes and how found
Undercut: correct causes and how found and measured
Lack of fusion: correct causes and that it is often hidden
Cracks: correct causes and suitable tests
Links each fault to visual or a suitable NDT method

essays.stem: Compare visual inspection, dye penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic and radiographic testing of welds. Say what each can find and one limit of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Visual inspection is quick and cheap and finds surface faults such as undercut, porosity, overlap and wrong weld size, but it cannot see inside the weld. Dye penetrant shows cracks and pores that break the surface, and works on stainless steel and aluminium, but it finds nothing below the surface and needs a clean surface. Magnetic particle testing uses a magnetic field and iron powder to show cracks at or just under the surface; it is quick on steel but only works on magnetic materials. Ultrasonic testing sends sound waves through the weld and finds hidden faults such as lack of fusion and cracks, and gives their depth; it needs a trained, qualified operator and is harder on thin or rough parts. Radiography uses X-rays or gamma rays to make a picture of the inside, and is good at showing porosity and slag; it needs strict radiation safety and a qualified operator, and is slow and costly.
markingPoints: Visual: finds surface faults; cannot see inside
Dye penetrant: surface-breaking faults on any non-porous metal; surface only
Magnetic particle: surface and near-surface on magnetic steel only
Ultrasonic: hidden faults and depth; needs qualified operator
Radiography: internal picture; radiation safety, cost and qualified operator

essays.stem: A weld on a fabricated tank stand fails visual inspection because of a crack. Describe how you would deal with it, from finding it to closing it out.
essays.modelAnswer: I mark the crack clearly on the part with paint marker and label the part as rejected, so nobody paints, ships or loads it. I stop any further work on that joint. I write a non-conformance report giving the job, the weld number from the weld map, the fault and its size, the requirement it does not meet, the date and my name. I tell the supervisor or person in charge at once. A crack is never accepted, so the decision is to repair it. The repair method is agreed: find the ends of the crack with dye penetrant, remove it fully to sound metal, check with dye penetrant, and reweld to the WPS by a qualified welder. I try to find the cause, such as fast cooling or damp electrodes, and check similar welds. When the repair is done, I inspect it again to the same standard. If it passes, I record the result, sign the NCR as closed and remove the reject label.
markingPoints: Marks and labels the part; stops further work on it
Writes an NCR with weld number, fault, requirement and date
Reports at once and agrees the repair method
Looks for the cause and checks similar welds
Re-inspects to the same standard and closes the NCR

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a dimensional inspection of a welded steel frame against its drawing: the tools, the checks, the tolerances and how you record them.
essays.modelAnswer: I wait until the frame has cooled and is resting on level supports, so it is not twisted by its own weight. I use a calibrated steel tape, a steel rule, a square, a spirit level, a straight edge and a string line. From the drawing I list the key sizes and their tolerances, or the general tolerance in the title block. I measure the overall length, width and height, the positions of brackets and holes from the datum, and the hole sizes. I measure both diagonals to check it is square, and check flatness with a string line or straight edge and twist by sighting across. Each reading is written against the drawing size on the inspection sheet, with pass or fail. Any size outside the tolerance is marked on the frame and raised as a non-conformance. I note which tape I used and sign and date the sheet.
markingPoints: Measures when cool, on level supports
Uses suitable, calibrated tools
Checks key sizes and positions from datums against tolerances
Checks squareness by diagonals and flatness or twist
Records each reading, pass or fail, tool used, and raises out-of-tolerance items

essays.stem: Using a weld map, explain how you would record and report the inspection of every weld on a fabricated steel tank stand, so that each weld can be traced later.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with a copy of the general arrangement drawing and give every weld a number, for example W1 to W40. That is the weld map. I make an inspection record with a line for each weld number. For each weld I record the welder's name or stamp number, the date, the WPS used, the electrode batch, and the results: size, visual faults, and any NDT done with its report number. If a weld is rejected, the line shows the NCR number and, later, the repair and re-inspection result. The record also lists the steel heat numbers and mill certificates for the main members. When the job is finished, I write a short report for the supervisor and client: the scope of inspection, the number of welds inspected, the number rejected and repaired, any parts not inspected, and the final result. The weld map, records and report are signed, dated and kept in the job file.
markingPoints: Numbers every weld on a drawing to make the weld map
Records welder, date, WPS, batch and results against each number
Links rejects to NCRs, repairs and re-inspections
Records material traceability
Writes a signed summary report and files the records

essays.stem: Explain the hazards an inspector faces in a working fabrication shop and on site, and how each is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Arc light from nearby welding can burn the eyes and skin, so the inspector wears safety glasses with side shields, uses a filter lens when watching a welder and stays behind screens. Hot welds and plates can burn without looking hot, so the inspector checks with a temperature crayon or waits, and wears gloves. Grinding sparks and flying slag can hit the eyes, so eye protection is always worn. Inspection chemicals, such as dye penetrant aerosols, are flammable and harmful to breathe, so they are used with ventilation, away from arcs and sparks, with the gloves the SDS names. Fume in enclosed tanks is dangerous, so confined spaces are entered only with a permit and gas testing. On site, inspection at height is done from a tagged scaffold or platform, with a harness where required. Lifted loads and moving cranes are a hazard, so the inspector never stands under a load. Radiography areas are kept clear while testing is going on.
markingPoints: Arc light: eye and skin protection and screens
Hot work and sparks: gloves, eye protection, checking temperature
Chemicals: ventilation, no ignition, PPE from the SDS
Confined spaces and heights: permits, gas testing, tagged access, harness
Lifting and radiography: keep clear of loads and controlled areas

practical1.title: Plan and carry out a full inspection of a welded fabrication against its drawing, with a weld map and NCRs
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a welded steel fabrication (for example a small frame or bracket assembly) made earlier, with some faults planted in it, together with its drawing and the acceptance limits for the job. As a group, write a short inspection plan: the checks, the tools, the limits and who does each part. Number every weld on a copy of the drawing to make a weld map. Each member then inspects some of the welds: cleans them, checks size with a fillet gauge, and looks for undercut, porosity, cracks, overlap, arc strikes and incomplete fill, recording each result against the weld number. Two members carry out the dimensional checks: key sizes, positions, diagonals and flatness. Choose two welds for dye penetrant testing and carry it out as the kit's instructions say. Mark every reject on the part, write an NCR for each, and put a reject label on the part. Finish with a short signed inspection report. Photograph each stage and add the photos, the weld map, the records, the NCRs and the report to the group's practical.
materials: A welded steel fabrication with planted faults, its drawing and the acceptance limits
Fillet weld gauges, a steel rule, tape measure, square, straight edge and string line
Dye penetrant kit (cleaner, penetrant, developer) and rags
Paint markers, reject labels, inspection record sheets, NCR forms and report sheet
photos: The group's inspection plan and the weld map
A member measuring a fillet weld with a gauge
A fault found, with the weld number marked beside it
Dye penetrant developed on a tested weld
The completed inspection records and NCRs
The part with its reject label and marked faults
checklist: Helped write the plan and the weld map
Used the fillet gauge correctly and recorded the right sizes
Found and correctly named the planted faults in their welds
Took dimensional readings accurately and judged them against the tolerances
Carried out dye penetrant testing in the correct steps
Made correct accept or reject decisions against the stated limits
Wrote a clear NCR for a reject
Signed and dated records and left the area clean
safety: Use dye penetrant sprays in a ventilated area, away from arcs and sparks, with the gloves the SDS names
Wear safety glasses throughout; welding may be going on nearby
Check parts are cool before handling and watch for sharp edges and spatter
Lift heavy parts with help or a hoist; do not lift alone

practical2.title: Goods-in, fit-up and in-process inspection for a welding job, with a hold point sign-off
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a small welding job with a WPS: a delivery of plate and section with mill certificates (some details deliberately wrong), packets of electrodes or wire (one damaged), and four or five butt and fillet joints already tacked up, some with faults such as a wrong root gap, a wrong bevel, misalignment or a cracked tack. As a group, first carry out a goods-in inspection: check sizes with a vernier and tape, check heat numbers against the certificates and check the consumables against the WPS. Quarantine and record anything that fails. Then each member inspects at least one fit-up against the WPS: bevel angle, root face, root gap, alignment, cleanliness and tacks, records the readings and decides whether to sign the hold point. Finally, while a welder (a member or the assessor) welds one approved joint, two members check and record the preheat with a temperature crayon (if the WPS asks for it), the current against the WPS, and the cleaning between runs. Photograph each stage and add the photos and records to the group's practical.
materials: Plate and section with mill certificates, some details wrong, prepared by the assessor
Packets of electrodes or wire, one damaged, and a WPS for the job
Four or five tacked-up joints with planted fit-up faults
Vernier caliper, tape, bevel protractor or weld gauge, hi-lo gauge, root gap gauges or feeler gauges
Temperature crayons, a welding machine with a current display or clamp meter, and welding PPE
Goods-in record, fit-up record with hold point boxes, in-process record and quarantine labels
photos: The delivery laid out with the certificates and the goods-in record
A plate being measured with a vernier
A member measuring a root gap or bevel angle
The completed fit-up record with hold points signed or refused
The preheat being checked with a crayon or the current being read
The completed in-process record and the cleaned work area
checklist: Checked sizes, heat numbers and certificates correctly
Checked consumables against the WPS and their condition
Quarantined and recorded failed items correctly
